# Probability spaces and events

Probability has to say which outcomes and which events are being discussed. On a finite set every subset can be an event. On an uncountable set, a sigma-algebra is a collection large enough for the countable operations the later arguments use.

Finite sample spaces, equally likely outcomes, the elementary axioms, conditional probability, and independence of events are on [Random experiments and probability](prob-01-experiments.qmd). This page keeps those identities and adds the sigma-algebra, countable additivity in the form needed for tail events, continuity along monotone sequences, and the Borel–Cantelli lemmas. The random variables built on this space are on [Random variables and laws](sp-10-random-variables.qmd).

## Outcomes and events

A sample space $\Omega$ is the set of elementary outcomes. An event is a subset of $\Omega$. The complement $A^c$ is the event that $A$ does not occur, the union $A\cup B$ is the event that at least one occurs, and the intersection $A\cap B$ is the event that both occur. Disjoint events have empty intersection. A partition is a family of disjoint events whose union is $\Omega$. Conditioning on the cells of a partition turns one probability into a sum of simpler ones, which is the [law of total probability](prob-01-experiments.qmd#thm-total-probability).

::: {#def-sp-probability-space .definition}
## Probability space

A sigma-algebra $\mathcal{F}$ on $\Omega$ contains $\Omega$, is closed under complements, and is closed under countable unions. It is then closed under countable intersections, by taking complements. A probability measure $\mathrm{P}:\mathcal{F}\to[0,1]$ satisfies $\mathrm{P}(\Omega)=1$ and is countably additive: for pairwise disjoint events $A_n\in\mathcal{F}$,

$$
\mathrm{P}\Bigl(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n\Bigr)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mathrm{P}(A_n).
$$

The triple $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathrm{P})$ is a probability space. The probability of an event $A$ is written $\Pr(A)$ as well as $\mathrm{P}(A)$.

:::

The three axioms on [Random experiments and probability](prob-01-experiments.qmd#def-probability-measure) are this definition specialised to the events that page uses. Closure under countable unions is what makes an event such as "infinitely many of the $A_n$ occur" an event. That event is

$$
\limsup_{n\to\infty} A_n=\bigcap_{m\ge 1}\bigcup_{n\ge m} A_n,
$$

the event that belongs to every tail union. It is the event in the Borel–Cantelli lemmas.

## Generated and Borel sigma-algebras

The sigma-algebra generated by a collection $\mathcal{C}$, written $\sigma(\mathcal{C})$, is the smallest sigma-algebra containing $\mathcal{C}$. For a single set $A$ it is $\{\emptyset, A, A^c, \Omega\}$, with duplicates removed if $A$ is empty or all of $\Omega$. For two sets $A$ and $B$, the four atoms

$$
A\cap B,\qquad A\cap B^c,\qquad A^c\cap B,\qquad A^c\cap B^c
$$

form a partition of $\Omega$. Every set in $\sigma(A,B)$ is a union of some of these atoms.

On $\mathbb{R}$, the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$ is the sigma-algebra generated by the open intervals. It contains the closed intervals, the half-open intervals, and every countable set, because each singleton is the intersection of a shrinking sequence of open intervals. Calling a set a Borel event says that it belongs to this sigma-algebra. It does not say that every subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is Borel.

## Consequences of the axioms

Countable additivity implies the properties already listed for a finite experiment, and two limit properties that need the countable axiom.

$\mathrm{P}(\emptyset)=0$, because $\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldots$ is a disjoint sequence whose union is $\emptyset$, so $\mathrm{P}(\emptyset)=\sum\mathrm{P}(\emptyset)$ forces the value $0$. Finite additivity is countable additivity with the later sets empty. If $A\subset B$, then $B=A\cup(B\setminus A)$ is a disjoint union, so $\mathrm{P}(A)\le\mathrm{P}(B)$. The inclusion-exclusion identity

$$
\mathrm{P}(A\cup B)=\mathrm{P}(A)+\mathrm{P}(B)-\mathrm{P}(A\cap B)
$$

is the same rearrangement as on the experiments page: add the two probabilities, and put back the overlap that was counted twice.

The union bound replaces an overlapping union by a larger disjoint one. Define $B_1=A_1$ and $B_n=A_n\setminus(A_1\cup\cdots\cup A_{n-1})$. The $B_n$ are disjoint, their union equals $\bigcup A_n$, and $B_n\subset A_n$, so

$$
\mathrm{P}\Bigl(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n\Bigr)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mathrm{P}(B_n)\le\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mathrm{P}(A_n).
$$

If $A_n\uparrow A$, meaning $A_n\subset A_{n+1}$ and $\bigcup_n A_n=A$, continuity from below says $\mathrm{P}(A_n)\uparrow\mathrm{P}(A)$. The increments $A_1$, $A_2\setminus A_1$, $A_3\setminus A_2$, $\ldots$ are disjoint and sum to $A$, so $\mathrm{P}(A)=\mathrm{P}(A_1)+\sum_{n\ge 2}\mathrm{P}(A_n\setminus A_{n-1})$, and the partial sum of that series is $\mathrm{P}(A_n)$.

If $A_n\downarrow A$, continuity from above says $\mathrm{P}(A_n)\downarrow\mathrm{P}(A)$. Apply continuity from below to the complements: $A_n^c\uparrow A^c$, so $\mathrm{P}(A_n^c)\uparrow\mathrm{P}(A^c)$, and subtract from $1$. For a probability the first set automatically has finite measure, which is the extra hypothesis the same argument needs for a general measure.

## Borel–Cantelli

::: {#thm-sp-borel-cantelli .theorem}
## Borel–Cantelli lemmas

If $\sum_n\mathrm{P}(A_n)<\infty$, then $\mathrm{P}(A_n\text{ infinitely often})=0$. If the events $A_n$ are independent and $\sum_n\mathrm{P}(A_n)=\infty$, then $\mathrm{P}(A_n\text{ infinitely often})=1$.

:::

For the first statement, the union bound on the tail gives

$$
\mathrm{P}\Bigl(\bigcup_{n\ge m} A_n\Bigr)\le\sum_{n\ge m}\mathrm{P}(A_n).
$$

The right-hand side tends to $0$ as $m\to\infty$ whenever the series converges. The event that infinitely many $A_n$ occur is contained in every tail union, so its probability is $0$. Equivalently, the tail unions decrease to that event, and continuity from above passes the limit inside $\mathrm{P}$. Independence is not used.

For the second statement, independence turns the probability of a long run of failures into a product. For $N\ge m$,

$$
\mathrm{P}\Bigl(\bigcap_{n=m}^{N} A_n^c\Bigr)=\prod_{n=m}^{N}\bigl(1-\mathrm{P}(A_n)\bigr)\le\exp\Bigl(-\sum_{n=m}^{N}\mathrm{P}(A_n)\Bigr),
$$

because $1-x\le e^{-x}$ for $x\in[0,1]$. If the series of probabilities diverges, the exponent tends to $-\infty$ as $N\to\infty$, and the probability that every $A_n$ with $n\ge m$ fails is $0$. Every tail therefore contains at least one occurrence, with probability $1$. That is the event of infinitely many occurrences.

Divergence without independence does not give the second conclusion. Repeat one event $A$ of probability $1/2$ at every $n$. The probabilities sum to infinity, and $\{A_n\text{ infinitely often}\}=A$ still has probability $1/2$.

## Conditional probability and independence

When $\mathrm{P}(B)>0$,

$$
\mathrm{P}(A\given B)=\frac{\mathrm{P}(A\cap B)}{\mathrm{P}(B)}.
$$

This is the definition on [Random experiments and probability](prob-01-experiments.qmd#def-conditional-probability). If $(B_i)$ is a finite or countable partition into events of positive probability,

$$
\mathrm{P}(A)=\sum_i\mathrm{P}(A\given B_i)\,\mathrm{P}(B_i).
$$

Bayes' rule divides one term of that sum by the whole sum:

$$
\mathrm{P}(B_j\given A)=\frac{\mathrm{P}(A\given B_j)\,\mathrm{P}(B_j)}{\sum_i\mathrm{P}(A\given B_i)\,\mathrm{P}(B_i)}.
$$

The formulas are identities for events. They do not require a density. The density form used to update a prior is on [Bayesian foundations](bayes-01-foundations.qmd#thm-bayes-rule).

Two events are independent when $\mathrm{P}(A\cap B)=\mathrm{P}(A)\mathrm{P}(B)$, the definition on [Random experiments and probability](prob-01-experiments.qmd#def-independent-events). For a collection, pairwise independence is weaker than mutual independence. For three events, the three pairwise product formulas do not imply $\mathrm{P}(A\cap B\cap C)=\mathrm{P}(A)\mathrm{P}(B)\mathrm{P}(C)$.

::: {#exm-sp-pairwise .example}
## Pairwise, and not mutual

Let $U$ and $V$ be independent fair bits, and set $A=\{U=1\}$, $B=\{V=1\}$, and $C=\{U\neq V\}$.

**Question.** Check pairwise independence, and check mutual independence.

**Solution.** Each of $A$, $B$, and $C$ has probability $1/2$. Also $\mathrm{P}(A\cap B)=\mathrm{P}(U=V=1)=1/4=\mathrm{P}(A)\mathrm{P}(B)$. The same count gives $\mathrm{P}(A\cap C)=\mathrm{P}(U=1,V=0)=1/4$ and $\mathrm{P}(B\cap C)=1/4$. Every pair is independent. The triple intersection $A\cap B\cap C$ requires $U=V$ and $U\neq V$, so it is empty and has probability $0$, not $1/8$. The three events are not mutually independent.

The second Borel–Cantelli lemma assumes independence of the family used in the product, not only pairwise products. A pairwise condition would not justify writing the probability of the intersection as the product over the whole tail.

:::

## Countable operations on a sequence of events

For a sequence of events $A_n$:

- at least one occurs on $\bigcup_n A_n$;
- all of them occur on $\bigcap_n A_n$;
- infinitely many occur on $\limsup_n A_n=\bigcap_m\bigcup_{n\ge m} A_n$;
- all but finitely many occur on $\liminf_n A_n=\bigcup_m\bigcap_{n\ge m} A_n$.

The limsup asks for an occurrence in every tail. The liminf asks for one tail in which every event occurs. Almost-sure convergence is a statement that a limsup of deviation events has probability $0$, which is why the first Borel–Cantelli lemma is the bridge from a summable series of probabilities to a pathwise limit on [Expectation and convergence](sp-11-convergence.qmd).

::: {.callout-note}
## Key idea
A probability space is a sample space, a sigma-algebra of events, and a countably additive probability. Countable unions make tail events measurable. If the probabilities of $A_n$ sum to a finite number, only finitely many occur, with probability $1$. If the events are independent and the probabilities sum to infinity, infinitely many occur, with probability $1$.
:::
